headline: Stennis engineer moves into civil service after years supporting rocket tests
standfirst: Kristie Foster’s new role preserves engineering experience at the Mississippi propulsion-testing center.
body:
Quality engineer Kristie Foster has become a civil servant at Stennis Space Center after working as a contractor supporting the center since 2008. She was hired in June as part of an effort to strengthen technical expertise within the civil service workforce.

Her responsibilities include quality assurance at the facilities that supply high-pressure gases and industrial water for rocket-engine testing. The gas system serves the site through a seven-mile pipeline, while the water facility draws on a 66-million-gallon reservoir for cooling and sound suppression.

Foster also supports safety work at the Thad Cochran Test Stand, where Blue Origin plans second-stage hot-fire testing for its New Glenn rocket. Her duties include reviewing test preparations and checking that operational plans are carried out correctly.

Her route to the role included community college, a university degree in construction management and land development, and internships at Stennis. The new appointment retains experience developed across years of work at the propulsion test site.

headline: Robotics team tests how machines could work alongside astronauts
standfirst: A Houston test facility is helping engineers adapt robotic arms and humanoid machines for tasks in space habitats.
body:
Engineers at Johnson Space Center are developing robots designed to handle practical tasks alongside astronauts, from moving cargo to inspecting equipment. Their focus is on improving the reliability of machines working in environments built for people.

The 16-member Dexterous Robotics Team combines mechanical, electronic and software expertise. Its experience includes Robonaut 2, which took part in technology demonstrations aboard the International Space Station, and the bipedal robot Valkyrie.

The team’s iMETRO facility brings together simulations, habitat mockups, robots and an outdoor testing area. Engineers can evaluate complete machines or individual components before considering them for exploration missions.

In one demonstration, software from PickNik enabled a robotic arm to identify and open a spacecraft hatch before moving cargo bags. Another project used a commercial arm and camera to inspect a freezer similar to those on the station.

The work currently emphasizes technologies relevant to a sustained lunar presence, with potential applications for future Mars missions.

headline: New mapping method reveals nearly 2,000 valleys beneath Greenland’s ice
standfirst: Researchers used subtle patterns on the ice surface to trace buried terrain and extend the known reach of many valleys.
body:
A new analysis has mapped 1,943 valleys beneath Greenland’s ice sheet, revealing a landscape that remains hidden from direct observation. About a third of the valleys were newly identified.

The technique, called Ice Flow Perturbation Analysis, uses small changes in the ice surface to infer the shape of underlying rock. Satellite observations provide the surface detail needed for that analysis.

The findings indicate that many previously mapped valleys extend farther into Greenland’s interior than existing datasets show. In some cases, those extensions stretch hundreds of kilometers. The study was published in Geophysical Research Letters.

Some features fit established explanations of Greenland’s geological history. Others raise questions, including long, similarly aligned valleys in the west-central region that suggest a possible tectonic influence.

Better knowledge of this terrain could help improve ice-flow projections. Valleys channel moving ice, so their location and shape are relevant to understanding how changes may spread inland as the ice sheet retreats.

headline: Starliner development briefing scheduled for September 28
standfirst: NASA and Boeing leaders plan to discuss the spacecraft’s progress and future crew flights.
body:
NASA and Boeing have scheduled a briefing on Starliner’s development for 3 p.m. EDT on Monday, September 28. The announced discussion will cover plans for regular crew flights to and from the International Space Station.

The briefing is set to take place at Kennedy Space Center in Florida, with online viewing available through NASA’s live coverage. Media already accredited for Crew-13 can participate in person.

The announcement, published on September 25, set out arrangements for journalists to join the call and submit questions. It did not itself provide the development update. Further details were expected at the scheduled briefing.

headline: San Marino joins Artemis Accords as 76th signatory
standfirst: The agreement was signed in Rimini, adding another country to the international framework for space exploration.
body:
San Marino became the 76th country to sign the Artemis Accords at a ceremony in Rimini on September 25. Industry and Technological Research Minister Rossano Fabbri signed for the republic.

The event was attended by NASA Europe representative Gregory Mann and the U.S. consul general in Florence, Joseph Tordella. The signing adds San Marino to a framework intended to support peaceful and coordinated exploration of space.

The accords were established in 2020 by NASA, the U.S. State Department and seven other founding nations. They set out practical principles for cooperation as governments and private organizations pursue activities on the Moon, Mars and beyond.

Participation can create opportunities for future collaboration, including scientific payloads and technology demonstrations. The signing announcement did not identify a specific San Marino flight or payload commitment.
